title_en: Stephen Hawking: Looking at the Stars
description_ru: Биография Стивена Хокинга: учёба, тяжёлая болезнь, открытие излучения чёрных дыр, книга «Краткая история времени» и чувство юмора.
text:
Stephen Hawking was one of the most famous scientists of the twentieth century, but he did not look like a typical genius. For most of his adult life he sat in a wheelchair and spoke through a computer. Even so, he explained black holes, the beginning of the universe and the nature of time to millions of ordinary people, and he did it with a wonderful sense of humour.

He was born on 8 January 1942 in Oxford, exactly three hundred years after the death of Galileo. He liked to mention this coincidence in interviews. His parents were both educated, and the house was full of books, although it was also rather untidy. At school Stephen was not an outstanding student at first. He was nicknamed "Einstein" by his classmates as a joke, because his marks were so ordinary. Nevertheless, he loved taking things apart to see how they worked, and with a friend he built a simple computer out of old clock parts.

He wanted to study mathematics at Oxford, but his father hoped that he would choose medicine. In the end he studied physics, since the university did not offer a mathematics course at his college. Hawking later admitted that he did very little work there. He estimated that he studied for about one hour a day, and he spent much of his time rowing and playing games. He still finished with a good enough degree to continue his studies at Cambridge.

At Cambridge, at the age of twenty-one, Hawking began to notice that his body was not working properly. He fell down stairs, he found it difficult to tie his shoes, and his speech became unclear. Doctors told him that he had a serious illness of the nerves, called motor neurone disease, and they believed that he would live for only two more years. He was deeply depressed. He later said that the news had a surprising effect, however. If life was going to be short, he thought, every day mattered, and he began to work much harder than before.

In 1965 he married Jane Wilde, and they had three children. His career grew quickly. He worked with the mathematician Roger Penrose to show that the universe probably started from a single point called a singularity. In 1974 he made his most important discovery. Using ideas from quantum physics, he showed that black holes are not completely black. They slowly send out a faint glow, which is now called Hawking radiation, and over very long periods they can even disappear. Scientists were astonished.

In 1979 he was appointed Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge, a post that Isaac Newton had once held. By then he could hardly speak, and he depended on his students and family to understand him. In 1985 he caught pneumonia and needed an operation that took away his voice altogether. A computer expert designed a speech synthesiser for him, and he controlled it at first with a small movement of his hand and later with a muscle in his cheek. The robotic American voice became his trademark, and he refused to change it, even when better ones were available.

Hawking wanted to share his ideas, so in 1988 he published "A Brief History of Time". The publisher warned him that every equation would halve the number of readers, so he included only one, the famous E = mc squared. The book was a huge success. It stayed on the bestseller lists in Britain for more than four years and has sold over ten million copies, although many people admit that they have not finished it. He also appeared in television programmes, and he even played himself in "The Simpsons" and "Star Trek".

He also had a playful side. He enjoyed friendly bets with his colleagues. In 1975 he bet his friend Kip Thorne that a star system called Cygnus X-1 was not a black hole, and when the evidence proved him wrong, he paid with a subscription to a magazine of Thorne's choice. In 2009 he held a party for time travellers, but he only sent out the invitations after the party had finished. Nobody came, which he took as proof that time travel is impossible.

Hawking never stopped being curious or funny. In 2007 he experienced weightlessness on a special aircraft, and he said it was one of the best moments of his life. He also warned that people should look after the planet, and he insisted that science must be explained simply. When he died on 14 March 2018, at the age of seventy-six, he was buried near Isaac Newton in Westminster Abbey. His message to young people was simple: "Look up at the stars and not down at your feet."

questions.question: What did doctors tell Hawking when he was twenty-one?
questions.answer: He had motor neurone disease and would live only about two more years.

questions.question: What is Hawking radiation?
questions.answer: The faint glow that black holes slowly send out, so they are not completely black.

questions.question: Why did the book include only one equation?
questions.answer: The publisher warned that every equation would halve the number of readers.

questions.question: What happened at the party for time travellers?
questions.answer: Nobody came, because he sent the invitations after the party.
